chapter_title: Chapter 2 (General Section): Underwriting and Rate Making

questions.text: The price of a given unit of insurance is called:
questions.explanation: RATE is defined as the price of a given unit of insurance. It is the cost charged per unit of coverage. The total premium is then calculated as: Premium = Sum Insured × Rate.

questions.text: The maximum amount that an insurance company will INDEMNIFY to someone who files a claim is called:
questions.explanation: SUM INSURED is the MAXIMUM AMOUNT that an insurance company will indemnify (pay) as per the policy conditions. It is the upper ceiling on the insurer's liability — the insurer will not pay beyond this amount regardless of the actual loss.

questions.text: The BASIC OBJECTIVE of Rate Making in insurance is:
options: To ensure the price of insurance is as high as possible
To ensure the price of insurance is adequate and reasonable
To ensure the insurer always earns maximum profit
To make insurance affordable only for the poor
questions.explanation: The BASIC OBJECTIVE of the rate making process is to ensure that the PRICE OF INSURANCE IS ADEQUATE AND REASONABLE — meaning the premium charged should be fair, correct, and justified for both the insurer and the insured. Not excessively high or dangerously low.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a source of information for the Underwriter?
options: Pre-Acceptance Risk Survey of the asset
questions.explanation: The REGISTRATION CERTIFICATE OF THE INSURER is NOT a source of information for the underwriter. It is the insurer's own document and is irrelevant to assessing a risk. Valid underwriting sources are: (1) Annual Accounts of the Proposer, (2) Pre-Acceptance Risk Survey of the asset, and (3) Proposal Form.

questions.text: Hazards in insurance are best described as:
options: Factors that only increase the frequency of loss
Factors that only increase the impact of loss
Factors that increase both the impact and frequency of loss
Factors that reduce the chance of loss
questions.explanation: HAZARDS are conditions that increase BOTH the impact (severity) and the frequency of loss. They raise the probability that a loss will occur AND/OR increase how large the resulting damage will be. Both dimensions — frequency and impact — are characteristics of a hazard.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding Physical Hazard?
options: Physical Hazards are unknown for rate making
Physical Hazards can be calculated from the balance sheet
Physical Hazards can be ascertained from information given in the Proposal Form
questions.explanation: Physical Hazard CAN BE ASCERTAINED (identified and assessed) from the information given in the PROPOSAL FORM. Physical hazards are tangible, observable conditions — they are not unknown or hidden. The proposal form contains details about the property, location, usage etc. that reveal physical hazards.

questions.text: Installation of a sprinkler system in the premises will:
options: Neither increase nor decrease the risk
questions.explanation: Installing a SPRINKLER SYSTEM in the premises DECREASES THE RISK. A sprinkler system helps control and extinguish fires quickly, reducing both the probability of a fire spreading and the extent of damage. This is a positive physical feature that lowers fire hazard and may lead to a premium discount.

questions.text: The PRIMARY PURPOSE of inserting a Deductible or Excess Clause in an insurance policy is:
options: To eliminate the payment of small claims
questions.explanation: The primary purpose of a DEDUCTIBLE (or EXCESS CLAUSE) is to ELIMINATE SMALL CLAIMS. Under a deductible, the insured bears the initial portion of any loss, so they will not file trivial claims. This reduces administrative burden for the insurer and encourages the insured to take better care of insured property.

questions.text: No Claim Bonus (NCB) is awarded when:
options: The insured files a very large claim
No claim has been made during the policy year
The insured renews the policy for the first time
The insured pays the premium in advance
questions.explanation: NO CLAIM BONUS (NCB) is a benefit/discount given by the insurer to the insured when NO CLAIM has been made during the policy year. It rewards careful behaviour — for example, a car owner who has no accidents receives a premium discount on renewal.

questions.text: No Claim Bonus (NCB) is described as which of the following?
options: A minor administrative tool with limited impact
A powerful strategy to improve underwriting experience and an integral part of the rating system
A tool only used in life insurance
A penalty for making too many claims
questions.explanation: NCB is a POWERFUL STRATEGY to improve UNDERWRITING EXPERIENCE and forms an INTEGRAL PART OF THE RATING SYSTEM. It incentivises policyholders to avoid filing small claims, reduces claim frequency, and ultimately improves the insurer's loss ratios.

questions.text: In Motor Insurance, one of the Warranties is:
options: Vehicle should not be used for speed testing
Vehicle should not carry personal luggage
Vehicle should not be driven more than 200 km per day
questions.explanation: In Motor Insurance, a standard WARRANTY is that the VEHICLE SHOULD NOT BE USED FOR SPEED TESTING. This condition is expressly stated in the motor insurance policy and must be complied with. Violating this warranty can void the claim. The other options are not standard insurance warranties.

questions.text: Insured Declared Value (IDV) in Motor Insurance includes:
options: An arbitrary price chosen by the insured
questions.explanation: INSURED DECLARED VALUE (IDV) in motor insurance is based on the MANUFACTURER'S SELLING PRICE of the vehicle (adjusted for depreciation based on the vehicle's age). It represents the current market value and is the maximum amount payable in case of total loss or theft.

questions.text: Pure Premium, after being suitably loaded, increases because of the addition of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Pure Premium is LOADED by adding: (1) EXPENSES of the insurer, (2) RESERVES set aside for future liabilities, and (3) PROFIT MARGIN. After adding all these to the pure premium, the final chargeable premium is arrived at. Pure premium alone only covers expected losses.

questions.text: The process of classifying risk and deciding which category it falls into is important for:
questions.explanation: The process of CLASSIFYING RISK into different categories is critically important for RATE MAKING. The risk category a proposer falls into directly determines the premium rate charged. Higher-risk categories attract higher rates, while lower-risk categories attract lower rates or discounts.

questions.text: Who decides whether to accept or reject a risk in the underwriting process?
questions.explanation: The UNDERWRITER is the officer in the insurance company who decides whether to ACCEPT or REJECT (decline) a risk, and if accepted, at what rate and on what terms. The insurance agent (primary underwriter) only collects information — the final underwriting decision rests with the company's underwriter.
